newsitem.title: UK: Cherie Blair charts new course as UK's First Lady.
newsitem.headline: Cherie Blair charts new course as UK's First Lady.

text.p: She's intelligent, ambitious, successful and the wife of Britain's new prime minister.
But Cherie Blair, a top-notch lawyer who may become a High Court judge and a mother of three who has combined an active family life with a demanding career, is still an enigma to much of the public.
Despite a gruelling six-week election campaign, much of it spent at husband Tony Blair's side, little more is known about her than when he became leader of the Labour Party in the summer of 1994.

She has been constantly in the public eye, but has almost never given interviews. The Catholic daughter of television actor Tony Booth and now the wife of Britain's youngest prime minister this century, she has lived in the public shadow of the men in her life.
"I started out the daughter of someone. Now I am the wife of someone. I'll probably end up being the mother of someone," Cherie, 42, quipped in a rare public comment.
But her own achievements are formidable and impressive. She received a first in law from the London School of Economics and was the top of her year in the exams for the Bar.

As a Queen's Counsel, or senior lawyer, she earns an estimated 250,000 pounds ($400,000) a year, more than her husband. She says she wants to continue her career, becoming Britain's first full-time working mother in 10 Downing Street.

"I have worked for 20 years and I know that I want to carry on. But I also know that I want to be with my husband and to share things with him," she confessed in an anniversary edition of Prima, a women's magazine.
"The most important thing is to keep the family together. We want to keep life as normal as possible."

Blair supports her in her desire to continue working and sees no reason why his career should interfere with hers. By all accounts they are a happy, devoted couple, still as close to each other as when they married 17 years ago.
"I'm proud of what Cherie has achieved. I think if women want to stay at home and look after the children then that's great. But they should have a choice," Blair said.
"I don't see any reason why she should give up her job because of my position."

Family, career and politics are the basic ingredients of her life. The Blair children, Euan, 13, Nicky, 11, and Kathryn, nine, will become the youngest residents of 10 Downing Street for more than half a century.
There has been talk of a Camelot era in British politics, reminiscent of the Kennedy era in the 1960s, with the sounds of children filling the prime minister's residence.
Cherie says she hopes that she will be able to pass on what she learned as the daughter of a well-known father to her own children to help them to cope with life in the spotlight.
Although she is reported to be opinionated and highly political, she has kept her views to herself apart from her public opposition to sex discrimination and her interest in domestic violence cases.
Her politics are to the left of her husband's, whose manoeuvring of Labour to the centre secured its first victory after nearly 18 years in opposition.
She credits veteran Labour left-winger Tony Benn with inspiring her "in my quest for socialism".
A specialist in public and employment law, she has fought for the rights of battered wives and has been threatened by the husbands of some of her clients.

"I was grateful that I had court staff to protect me. My clients had to face the prospect of living with the threat and reality of violence at home, where there would be no one to protect them," she said after becoming a trustee of Refuge, a charity that shelters battered wives.
Cherie's early legal career paralleled her husband's. They started as trainee lawyers in the same office and married two years later.

Both had political ambitions. But after she was defeated for a parliamentary seat in 1983 whereas her husband was elected, she discarded her own political ambitions to concentrate on law and watch from the sidelines as he worked his way up.
Comparisons with U.S. First Lady Hillary Clinton are inevitable. Both women are very ambitious, highly successful lawyers, said by some to be the driving force behind their politician husbands.
But while Mrs Clinton has taken an active part in her husband's Cherie Blair has so far shown no indication that she plans to do the same.
